stops.name: Cádiz, the yellow fever and the father's legacy
stops.campa: The great yellow-fever epidemic of 1800 falls on Cádiz, and Bernardo falls with it. Ten thousand die around him; he lies at the door of death and is spared. As he rises, news crosses the ocean: Ambrosio O'Higgins, Viceroy of Peru, died in Lima on 18 March 1801, and at the very end, the father relented. A codicil recognizes the son and leaves him the hacienda of Las Canteras with its thousands of cattle. The father acknowledges the son only from the far side of the grave; they never exchanged a living word.

stops.name: Valparaíso, the homecoming
stops.campa: On 6 September 1802 the hills of Valparaíso rise out of the sea and Bernardo steps ashore in Chile after eight years, carrying Miranda's letter in the lining of his hat and his dead father's name newly his own. No one meets him; he is a stranger in his patria. The canon pauses on the image: the future Supreme Director standing unknown on the same shore from which he will one day launch the squadrons that free the Pacific.

stops.name: Chillán, the mother's embrace
stops.campa: He rides south to Chillán and after twelve years stands before doña Isabel Riquelme and his half-sister Rosa. The mother receives the son she surrendered as an infant; from this hour the three are never truly parted again: Isabel and Rosa will follow him over the cordillera into exile and to the end in Lima. Here he takes up publicly the name O'Higgins, the dead Viceroy's gift, and the canon notes the transformation: Bernardo Riquelme, the hidden child, has become don Bernardo O'Higgins, vecino of the south.

stops.name: Hacienda Las Canteras, taking possession
stops.campa: He takes possession of Las Canteras on the Isla de la Laja: leagues of pasture under the Antuco volcano, four thousand head of cattle, the frontier of Araucanía at the fence line. The disciple of Miranda becomes a farmer, and a good one: he plants vines, breeds horses, trades with the Pehuenche across the Biobío in their own tongue. The canon keeps this decade as the hidden years, the Liberator ploughing like Cincinnatus while the letter in the hat lining waits for its hour.

stops.name: Los Ángeles, alcalde and man of the frontier
stops.campa: The vecinos of the Laja make him alcalde of the cabildo of Los Ángeles and subdelegate of the frontier partido. He drains marshes, lays out roads, holds parleys with the caciques, and quietly measures the men around him against the coming test. Spain, meanwhile, decays audibly: the news of Trafalgar, then of the King's captivity at Bayonne, arrives over the cordillera like distant thunder. The canon shows him reading the gazettes at Las Canteras and writing to trusted friends that the hour Miranda foretold is drawing near.

stops.name: Las Canteras, the news of the Junta of Santiago
stops.campa: A rider brings word from the capital: on 18 September a Junta of Government has been sworn in Santiago in the name of the captive King. O'Higgins reads through the loyal formulas to the fire underneath: Miranda's fire. He arms his inquilinos, forms two militia companies of his own horsemen at his own cost, and drills them on the pastures of Las Canteras. The canon marks it precisely: while others debate, the man of the Laja is already raising the first soldiers of what will become the Army of Chile.

stops.name: Santiago, deputy in the first National Congress
stops.campa: On 4 July 1811 the first National Congress of Chile opens in Santiago and O'Higgins takes his seat as deputy for Los Ángeles. He sits with the exaltados, the party of full independence, and works the corridors with a paper hidden in his coat: the plan of secret organization he has drawn from Miranda's constitutions. It is O'Higgins, the canon holds, who gives the brotherhood its Chilean name: Lautaro, after the Mapuche boy who learned the conqueror's art and turned it against him. The huacho schooled among caciques names the revolution for one.

stops.name: El Roble on the Itata, the charge that made the general
stops.campa: At dawn on 17 October 1813 the royalists surprise the patriot camp at the Roble ford of the Itata. The line breaks; men drown in the river; the day is lost. Then O'Higgins arrives at the gallop, seizes the musket of a soldier shot dead beside him, and though a ball tears through his leg he stands in the ford and cries the words the nation will carve on his monuments. The routed army turns behind him and throws the royalists back across the river. From this wound and this cry, the canon dates his generalship.
stops.quote: ¡O vivir con honor, o morir con gloria! ¡El que sea valiente, que me siga!
stops.quote_source: Battle tradition of El Roble, 17 October 1813, as preserved by the Chilean Army and the chroniclers (Barros Arana, Historia General de Chile)

stops.name: Concepción, General in Chief of the Army
stops.campa: The Junta strips José Miguel Carrera of the command and gives it to the wounded colonel of El Roble. At Concepción O'Higgins takes up an army that is hungry, unpaid and half-shod, in a province the royalists are devouring from the sea. The Carreras never forgive him the promotion, and the canon opens here the fratricidal wound of the Patria Vieja: two houses, Carrera and O'Higgins, quarreling over the cradle of the republic while Abascal's regiments land from Peru.

stops.name: El Quilo and Membrillar, the two days on the Itata
stops.campa: On 19 and 20 March 1814 the war doubles its drumbeat: O'Higgins forces the crossing at El Quilo, and a day later stands with Mackenna in the entrenchments of Membrillar as Gaínza's whole army breaks against them. Powder smoke lies on the Itata for two days; the patriot squares hold. The canon pairs the battles like twin hinges: the moment the improvised militias of Chile prove they can stand in open field against the veterans of the King.

stops.name: Quechereguas, the road to Santiago barred
stops.campa: Gaínza slips north for Santiago; O'Higgins, outmarching him by forced night marches with an army on bleeding feet, throws himself across the road at the casas of Quechereguas on the Claro. On 8 April the royalists assault the position three times and three times are hurled back. The capital never sees the enemy. The canon loves the arithmetic of the feat, the slower army arriving first, and reads in it the O'Higgins signature: not elegance, but an immovable body placed between Chile and its destruction.

stops.name: The banks of the Lircay, the treaty signed under protest
stops.campa: On 3 May 1814, under the guns of the English commodore Hillyar's mediation, O'Higgins signs the Treaty of Lircay: Chile to acknowledge the King, the royalists to leave; hostages exchanged; the flags of the Patria Vieja furled. He signs as a soldier who cannot feed his men, and the canon absolves him with the sequel: the Viceroy in Lima repudiates the treaty within weeks and sends Osorio with fresh regiments. The parchment of Lircay becomes the proof text that with Spain there is no peace but submission: independence or nothing.
